---
title: "Poisson regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Poisson regression models a nonnegative count with a positive conditional mean. We use Nettle's ([1998](https://doi.org/10.1006/jaar.1998.0328)) country-level study of language diversity and climate. One row is one country; the response is its reported language count, mean growing season (MGS) is the ecological predictor, and area measures geographic opportunity. The prepared table comes from [Bodo Winter's course-data repository](https://github.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data/blob/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv). That repository states no data license, so these notes do not redistribute it.

The Poisson restriction equates conditional [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) with the conditional mean. Its [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the observed country totals fixed while comparing coefficient values, and its product assumes [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) across country rows after predictors. Shared regions, histories, and cross-border languages make that factorization a substantive approximation.

The main modeling decision is whether country area may be treated as proportional
exposure for a database count whose entries depend on geopolitical boundaries.
Defining that response and opportunity structure gives the coefficient its units
before the log-mean equation is fitted.

## What the country count measures {#nettle-country-language-measurement}

`Langs` is the source table's reported number of languages associated with a
country. The course file contains only that total; it has no language identifiers,
speaker counts, documentation records, or rule for distinguishing a language from
a variety. Country totals consequently do not partition a single list of languages.
A language used across a political border can contribute to more than one country
total, and this table cannot audit that overlap.

The row unit also matters. A country is a geopolitical aggregation whose borders,
settlement history, contact patterns, and documentation practices may all affect
the reported total. Mean growing season and area are country summaries attached to
that same unit. The analysis below asks whether the 74 represented country totals
vary with those summaries under a declared mean model. It does not sample
individual languages or language users.

| Stage | Quantity available here | Limit on the claim |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Source record | One reported language total per country | Language overlap and language-versus-variety decisions are unavailable. |
| Predictor record | Country mean growing season and geographic area | Neither variable is an assigned intervention. |
| Model row | One of 74 countries | Nearby countries and shared histories may remain dependent. |
| Fitted target | Conditional variation among represented country totals | The coefficient does not identify a climate mechanism or a population of independent languages. |

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-poisson
#| echo: true
path <- "data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  nettle <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/",
                "applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(digest::digest(source_file, "sha256", file = TRUE, serialize = FALSE) ==
    "3c5abfbec7b2132a9b81ee9a178cbd5559426578032b60c6c4ad74046898793b")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file)
  nettle <- data.frame(
    country = raw$Country, log10_population = raw$Population,
    log10_area_km2 = raw$Area, log_area_km2 = log(10) * raw$Area,
    mean_growing_season_months = raw$MGS, language_count = as.integer(raw$Langs)
  )
}
stopifnot(nrow(nettle) == 74L)
count_fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months,
                 family = poisson(link = "log"), data = nettle)
fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2),
           family = poisson(link = "log"), data = nettle)
```

The Algeria row makes the units visible. The source stores population and area on a base-ten log scale, while the offset requires a natural logarithm.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-nettle-country
transform(
  nettle[nettle$country == "Algeria", c(
    "country", "log10_population", "log10_area_km2", "log_area_km2",
    "mean_growing_season_months", "language_count"
  )],
  population = 10^log10_population,
  area_km2 = 10^log10_area_km2
)
```

Before using area, the count-only model states

$$
\log\lambda_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

Its mean is an expected language count per country. The offset model below asks a stronger rate question by assuming that expected count is proportional to geographic area.

The model is

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_i]=\operatorname{Var}[Y_i]=\lambda_i,
$$

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

Thus $\lambda_i/A_i=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i)$ is the fitted language rate per square kilometer.

The [Poisson distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution.qmd) adds more than count support: conditional on the predictors, its variance equals its mean. The log link keeps $\lambda_i$ positive and makes a coefficient additive in log rate, hence multiplicative after exponentiation. [Conditional independence](../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd) also requires the joint country-count distribution to factorize once MGS and area are supplied. Shared histories, cross-border languages, contact, and spatial proximity make that restriction substantive and checkable.

```{r}
#| label: nettle-poisson-summary
#| echo: true
c(mgs_coefficient = coef(fit)[["mean_growing_season_months"]],
  one_month_rate_ratio = exp(coef(fit)[["mean_growing_season_months"]]))
```

```{r}
#| label: nettle-poisson-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
nettle$observed_rate <- nettle$language_count / exp(nettle$log_area_km2)
grid <- data.frame(mean_growing_season_months =
                     seq(min(nettle$mean_growing_season_months),
                         max(nettle$mean_growing_season_months), length.out = 200L))
grid$fitted_rate <- exp(coef(fit)[[1L]] +
                          coef(fit)[["mean_growing_season_months"]] *
                          grid$mean_growing_season_months)
ggplot(nettle, aes(mean_growing_season_months, observed_rate)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = fitted_rate), color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Mean growing season (months)",
       y = "Languages per square kilometer") + theme_classic()
```

A one-month increase in MGS multiplies the fitted rate by `r round(exp(coef(fit)[[2L]]), 3)`, conditional on the fixed-area-exposure specification. Nettle instead estimated the log-area coefficient. Fixing it to one asserts that twice the area yields twice the expected reported country total at fixed MGS. The estimate therefore describes an area-normalized association among these 74 geopolitical records under that assumption; it supplies no climate intervention or sampling design for a causal claim.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which assumption is added when area becomes an offset rather than an estimated predictor?
2. Why does nonnegative-integer support not establish the Poisson variance restriction?
3. What does exponentiating the MGS coefficient produce?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The area coefficient is fixed at one on the log scale, so doubling area must double the expected count at fixed MGS. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. Many count distributions share the same support. Poisson additionally requires conditional mean and variance to be equal. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. It produces the fitted multiplicative change in expected count or rate for a one-month MGS increase, conditional on the remaining specification. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>
